input.question: Why does the human heart have blood vessels feeding it, when all the blood passes through it anyway?
input.ground_truth: The same reason why a water treatment plant has drinking fountains. The apparatus to deliver water/blood over a distance is different from what is need to pass it on to the end user. Blood cell zooming through a massive artery don't slow down enough for oxygen to be transfer, nor are artery walls adapted to that purpose. That is what capillaries are for.

Explain the following question in a simple way as if you are explaining to a 5-year-old.

Question: Why does the human heart have blood vessels feeding it, when all the blood passes through it anyway?

Answer:

response.prediction:
Okay, let’s imagine your heart is like a big playground slide.

The blood in your body is like all the kids who want to go down the slide. But the slide (the heart) itself also needs to stay strong and healthy, just like the playground needs to be taken care of.

So, the heart has its own little tiny slides—these are the blood vessels called arteries and veins. These tiny slides bring food and fresh air (which come in the blood) right to the heart muscle itself. That way, the heart can stay strong and keep working to pump blood to the rest of your body.

Even though the heart pumps blood everywhere, it still needs its own special food and oxygen, so that’s why it has its own blood vessels feeding it!
